sources.claim: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (last updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal nationwide, no legal gender recognition, LGBTI organisations can register; the country ranks among the most 'accepting' in the region in perception indices and surveys show strong support for an anti-discrimination law, but a 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found only 22% of Filipinos supported same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets; diversity-and-inclusion executive orders (2019, amended 2023) exist but were not implemented as of 2025; non-discrimination ordinances enacted at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels, while national SOGIE legislation has been filed repeatedly since 1999 but never passed; Anti-Bullying Act 2013 and the Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy (2017, reiterated 2022) cover SOGI in schools; Safe Spaces Act 2019 covers homophobic and transphobic slurs.

Bulatlat news (26 June 2025): an eighteen-year-old trans woman (Kierra Apostol, student of Cagayan State University, Peñablanca) was found dead in a Cagayan province river on 23 June 2025 with visible signs of physical assault; a person who admitted picking her up the previous night surrendered to police and denied killing her; the same piece records the killing of trans activist and former journalist Ali Macalintal by an unidentified gunman inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos (23 June) and of Shalani Dolina in Caloocan earlier in 2025; a national LGBT alliance says the violence is 'proof that LGBT persons remain unsafe' and demands passage of the SOGIESC Equality Bill, stuck in Congress for 25 years (latest version filed 2022 as House Bill 5551 / Senate Bill 1600).

The attached sources are national-level rather than regional: a country-organisation overview of the national legal picture, a June 2025 report on the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman in a different province (Cagayan), and a national news item on a case in another region (Batangas) that could not be retrieved at fetch time.

sources.claim: Outright International's Philippines country overview (updated 12 March 2026): same-sex conduct legal nationwide; no legal gender recognition (still required: no LGR pathway); Executive Order 100 s.2019 (signed 17 Dec 2019) created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, amended by EO 51 s.2023 to add a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee, neither implemented as of 2025; anti-discrimination ordinances exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels but national legislation filed since 1999 has not been enacted; a 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found 22% support for same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets.

Alternative-media report (26 June 2025): an 18-year-old trans woman, Kierra Apostol, was found dead with signs of physical assault in a river in Peñablanca, Cagayan province on 23 June 2025 after being missing since 22 June; her mother reported the disappearance to local police; Bahaghari (national LGBT alliance) chairperson called the killing part of a pattern of violence against Filipino trans women and renewed calls for the SOGIESC Equality Bill. Case is in Cagayan Valley region, not Caraga — national-climate evidence.

The country dossier located no province-specific trans ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding for this division; all three sources below are national-context legal and survey material that applies province-wide.

sources.claim: Korea Times (22 July 2024): the Seoul Central District Court ruled that a police officer's advice to an LGBTQ+ individual midway through legal gender change to "avoid using public restrooms for a while" infringed their personal rights; 300,000 won of a 3 million won claim awarded, final 2 July. Both first and second instances ruled for the plaintiff; the appellate court called comfortable restroom use "a fundamental and universal human right", and the officer received National Human Rights Commission human-rights education. Also cites the Commission's 2021 survey of 591 trans respondents (41% had used a restroom of a different gender than their identity out of fear; 39% avoided food and drinks; 36% forwent restroom use) and a 2021 Pohang branch ruling awarding 7 million won against an academy operator who barred a trans student from using restrooms.

NOTE: page body did not load at fetch time (navigation chrome only); the underlying Yonhap article (8 May 2024, tagged "legal sex change" / "transgender surgery") headlines a court ruling against mandating transgender surgery to change legal sex status — the national framework barring surgical requirements for legal gender recognition.

records.name: Tacna
records.current_summary: On 19 April 2025, Marcia Paucara Cora (48), a trans woman, was found dead by mechanical asphyxia (compression of the upper airways) in a hospedaje room in Tacna; she entered with a man who registered under a false identity, was filmed leaving in haste about two hours later, and remains unidentified despite camera footage and taxi-driver testimony. The case is being investigated as a possible hate crime (Wayka, Trome); the family and local LGBTQ collectives held a vigilia on 23 May demanding justice, describing the killing as "the reflection of a structural system of violence." This is the first documented such killing in this small border department. Under the single-incident rule, a lone killing moves a score only slightly unless patterned or state-implicated; here the perpetrator is unidentified and the state's response is active (hate-crime framing) though there is no hate-crime statute to charge under nationally.  Deviation: −0.02 from national 0.36. The justification is the per-capita impact in a small population (the department has a few hundred thousand inhabitants) where one killing is statistically notable, combined with the absence of a hate-crime enhancement meaning the legal response is identical to ordinary homicide. No facility ban, expression criminalisation, or police-targeting evidence specific to Tacna was found. The investigation-as-hate-crime posture is a marginally positive institutional signal.  vs Lima (0.33): Lima's multi-year concentration and 2025 case provide a thicker evidence base for a larger deduction. vs La Libertad (0.34): both are −0.02; La Libertad's 10-death dataset is far more robust but is partially offset by its protective ordinance, while Tacna's single case has no counterweight, netting them level.

sources.claim: Independent human-rights outlet Wayka (27 May 2025): investigation into the possible hate-crime killing of Marcia Paucara Cora, 48, a trans woman, found dead on 19 April in a hospedaje in Tacna; the necropsy confirmed death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the upper airways; the man who accompanied her registered under a false identity and fled; police hold camera footage and taxi-driver testimony but have not identified the suspect; a vigil on 23 May demanded justice and community organisations called it "the reflection of a structural system of violence"; the piece also records that Peru has no gender-identity law or hate-crime statute, and that a recently promulgated national law restricts public-bathroom access by sexual orientation.

Daily press (21 May 2025): detailed crime report - a trans woman of 48 found dead in hostal 'Los 5 Titos' on Calle Arias y Aragüez in central Tacna; she entered at 8:07 a.m. accompanied by a man who left alone about two hours later without his bag; necropsy confirmed asphyxia by compression of the upper airways as murder; police are tracking the suspect's escape route on CCTV; she was initially registered unidentified before the hostal cameras identified her; the family's wake was held at their home.
